chapter: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
title: Colored, Negro, Black, and Caldwell's mixed family
summary: They discuss changing racial terms and Caldwell says his Welsh-named mother's family looked white while his sister was dark.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: You know, now, it always seemed to me -- it always seems very funny when -- now, when you used to say people were colored, and then they say you've got to say Negro, which is Spanish for Black.
And now you have to say Black. Now, I can remember when -- when people referred to Blacks, that was really colonial talk.
I mean that was almost like saying the natives.

But they used to say the Blacks, and that was really insulting. But the thing about it, it seems -- I mean where is a person -- why is a person who is three quarters white called Black? Now, that don't make sense, does it?
You know? And I don't -- there are things about this that --
It is stupid because my mother, if I

would show you a picture, see, my name, that's a Welsh (unintelligible) name, Caldwell, actually. See? And on our side was white. See? When we were kids, they thought she was white. My two sisters, the oldest sister, she was dark brown skinned. They thought that she was one of the sisters.
